title: Because of That
theme: Cause and effect: triggers, influence and result words
objectives: I can name causes, triggers, and results using ten precise words.
I can tell the difference between a trigger, a contributing factor, and an outcome.
I can connect a cause to its result with thus, hence, and due to, in the right kind of sentence.
I can explain a chain of causes and effects in my own writing.
rationale: Cause-and-effect reasoning drives science and history texts, so this unit pairs the nouns and verbs of causation (outcome, trigger, contribute, influence, impact, provoke, originate) with the connectors that signal it in formal writing (thus, hence, due to). Students learn that causes differ in kind: something can begin a chain (originate), set it off (trigger), add to it (contribute), shape it (influence), or provoke a reaction, and the result can be named as an outcome or an impact. Three words (trigger, influence, impact) have a second familiar sense, so students also practice matching a word to its job in a sentence.

words.def: The result of an action, an event, or a process.
words.ex: The outcome of the vote surprised everyone, since the less popular idea won.
words.ex2: Three different experiments produced the same outcome.
words.nonExample: A plan that has not been carried out yet has no outcome so far.

apps.academic: A scientist records the outcome of every trial, even when it is not the one expected.
apps.spoken: What was the outcome of the game?
apps.writing: Use outcome for the final result of an event or a decision.

cloze.s: After a long debate, the ___ of the vote was a tie, so the club voted again.

cloze2.s: Because the experiment was repeated five times with the same result, scientists trusted the ___ more.

misuse.s: The outcome came first, before anything had happened to cause it.
misuse.why: An outcome is a result, so it comes after the event that causes it.

visual.alt: A finish line beside a bar chart.

words.def: To cause something to start, often suddenly.

senses.def: Something that sets off a reaction or an event.
senses.example: The first snowfall was the trigger that sent the deer down the mountain.

words.ex: A single spark can trigger a wildfire in dry grass.
words.ex2: The smell of baking bread triggered a memory of her grandmother's kitchen.
words.nonExample: A match that is never lit does not trigger a fire.

apps.academic: Historians name the event that triggered a war and separate it from the deeper causes.
apps.spoken: That song triggers so many memories.
apps.writing: Use trigger for the event that starts a chain of events.

cloze.s: In dry grass, one spark from a campfire can ___ a fast-spreading fire.

cloze2.s: Pollen in the air can ___ sneezing in people with allergies.

misuse.s: The alarm was triggered by a quiet day when nothing at all happened.
misuse.why: To trigger is to set something off; nothing happening sets nothing off.

visual.alt: A lightning bolt beside a ringing bell.

words.def: To give a part toward a result, a goal, or a shared effort.
words.ex: Careless littering contributes to dirty streams and parks.
words.ex2: Each student contributed one idea to the class mural.
words.nonExample: A person who watches and gives nothing is not contributing.

apps.academic: Many factors contribute to a change in climate, not just one.
apps.spoken: Everyone should contribute to the group project.
apps.writing: Use contribute for a share in a result, good or bad.

cloze.s: Late nights and skipped breakfasts both ___ to Dev's tiredness at school.

cloze2.s: Each family will ___ a dish to the neighborhood picnic, so there will be plenty to eat.

misuse.s: Jack contributed nothing to the project, so he deserves credit for its success.
misuse.why: To contribute is to give a part; someone who gave nothing did not contribute.

visual.alt: Puzzle pieces being added to a shared picture.

words.def: The power to affect what people think, do, or become, without using force.

senses.def: To affect or change what someone thinks or does.

words.ex: A good teacher can have a lasting influence on a student's future.
words.ex2: The weather has a strong influence on how many people visit the park.
words.nonExample: A rule nobody has heard of has no influence on how people behave.

apps.academic: Historians study how one writer's ideas had influence on later leaders.
apps.spoken: My cousin is a good influence on me.
apps.writing: Use influence for a power that shapes choices without force.

cloze.s: Reading about a scientist as a child had a strong ___ on Priya's decision to study biology.

cloze2.s: Friends can have a powerful ___ over the clothes we choose to wear.

misuse.s: Her influence over the club was so great that nobody paid attention to anything she said.
misuse.why: Influence is the power to affect others; if nobody pays attention, there is no influence.

visual.alt: A person at the center of a small group.

words.def: A strong effect that something has on a person, a place, or a situation.

senses.def: The force of one object hitting another.
senses.example: The impact of the ball cracked the window.

words.ex: The new library had a big impact on how much students read.
words.ex2: Plastic bags can have a harmful impact on ocean wildlife.
words.nonExample: A comment that nobody hears has no impact.

apps.academic: Scientists measure the impact of new farming methods on rivers.
apps.spoken: That story had a big impact on me.
apps.writing: Use impact for a strong effect, not for a tiny change.

cloze.s: The hurricane had a devastating ___ on the coastal town, destroying hundreds of homes.

cloze2.s: Recycling programs have a positive ___ on the amount of trash sent to landfills.

misuse.s: The storm had no impact, yet it destroyed every building in town.
misuse.why: Impact means a strong effect; destroying every building is a very strong effect.

visual.alt: A drop of water making ripples spread outward.

words.def: To cause a strong reaction, such as anger, laughter, or discussion.
words.ex: The mayor's comment provoked an angry response from teachers.
words.ex2: The mysterious painting provoked a lively debate among the students.
words.nonExample: A calm, friendly greeting does not provoke anger.

morph.note: A silent e is added at the end: vok -> voke.

apps.academic: A cartoonist may provoke readers to think about a problem.
apps.spoken: Don't provoke the neighbor's dog by shaking the fence.
apps.writing: Use provoke for causing a reaction, often a strong or negative one.

cloze.s: The unfair rule was sure to ___ complaints from students at every table in the cafeteria.

cloze2.s: The author hoped her surprising ending would ___ a long discussion in the book club.

misuse.s: The teacher's calm, kind greeting was meant to provoke the class to anger.
misuse.why: To provoke is to cause a strong reaction; a calm, kind greeting is not meant to anger anyone.

visual.alt: A ringing bell next to an angry face.

words.def: To begin or come into being at a certain time or place.
words.ex: The tradition originated in a small village and later spread across the country.
words.ex2: Many rivers originate in mountains, where rain and melting snow run downhill.
words.nonExample: A river's mouth, where it reaches the sea, is not where it originates.

apps.academic: Historians trace where an idea first originated before they follow how it spread.
apps.writing: Use originate for the place or time where something first began.

cloze.s: The rumor did not ___ with Ana; she had only heard it from a friend.

cloze2.s: Most rivers ___ in high ground, where rain and melting snow gather into small streams.

misuse.s: The idea originated at the end of the story, after the whole thing was already finished.
misuse.why: To originate is to begin; the end of a story is not where something begins.

visual.alt: A seedling next to a map pin.

words.def: As a result; for this reason.
words.ex: The road was flooded; thus, the buses took a different route.
words.ex2: The team practiced every day, and thus they were ready for the final.
words.nonExample: A sentence such as 'It is Tuesday; thus, frogs are green' misuses thus, because Tuesday does not cause green frogs.
words.rel: words that signal cause and result

apps.academic: In essays, thus connects a reason to its result in formal writing.
apps.spoken: Thus ends the story of how we got lost.
apps.writing: Use thus after a reason to introduce the result; it sounds more formal than so.

cloze.s: The bridge was closed for repairs; ___, drivers had to take a much longer road.

cloze2.s: Plants need light to make food; ___ a plant kept in a dark closet will weaken.

misuse.s: It rained all day; thus, the picnic was held in bright, dry sunshine.
misuse.why: Thus introduces a result of what came before; a sunny picnic is not a result of all-day rain.

visual.alt: A flow from a reason on the left to a result on the right, with thus on the arrow.

words.def: For this reason; which is why.
words.ex: Cats are quiet hunters, hence their reputation as sneaky animals.
words.ex2: The lake freezes in January, hence the town's famous ice festival.
words.nonExample: A sentence with no reason before 'hence' does not work, because the reader has nothing to connect it to.
words.rel: words that signal cause and result

apps.academic: Hence often appears in science and history writing to link a cause to a result.
apps.spoken: The cake had no sugar, hence the sour taste.
apps.writing: Use hence to explain why something has a certain name or result, especially in formal writing.

cloze.s: The soup had no salt; ___ the unhappy faces around the table.

cloze2.s: The creek runs red after every rain because of the clay soil, ___ its name, Red Creek.

misuse.s: The sky was clear all day, hence the heavy rain that soaked everyone.
misuse.why: Hence introduces a result of the reason before it; a clear sky does not cause heavy rain.

visual.alt: An arrow from a cause on the left to a result on the right, with hence as the label.

words.ex: The game was delayed due to a thunderstorm.
words.ex2: Her absence was due to a bad cold.
words.nonExample: 'The road was closed due to it was icy' is not correct; use because it was icy, or due to the ice.
words.rel: words that signal cause and result

apps.academic: Scientists write 'due to' followed by a noun to name a cause, such as due to rising temperatures.
apps.writing: Use due to before a noun phrase; use because before a full clause.

cloze.s: The picnic was canceled ___ heavy rain.

cloze2.s: Many flights were late ___ the snowstorm that closed the airport.

misuse.s: The grass was dry due to the heavy rain that had fallen all week.
misuse.why: Due to introduces a cause; heavy rain does not make grass dry.

passage.title: The Green Pond
paras: In May, the pond behind Westbrook Middle School turned bright green almost overnight. Students crowded along the fence, and the strange color provoked dozens of questions. Ms. Chavez's science class decided to find the cause.

First, they asked where the problem might originate. Sam noticed a drainage pipe that carried water from the athletic field into the pond. The groundskeeper confirmed that the field had been fertilized the week before. "Fertilizer helps grass grow," Sam said, "so maybe it helps other plants grow too."

Next, the class gathered more clues. Heavy rain had fallen two days after the fertilizer was spread, so the runoff carried some of it into the pond. Then a week of warm, sunny weather triggered a burst of algae growth. The students learned that sunlight and warm water have a strong influence on how fast algae multiply. Together, these causes contributed to the bloom.

The impact on the pond was easy to see. The thick green layer blocked sunlight from plants below the surface. When algae die, tiny organisms that break them down can use up much of the oxygen in the water. Fish and insects had less oxygen to breathe, and thus the pond's animals were in danger. Ms. Chavez asked the class to explain the chain from start to finish. "Rain moved fertilizer into the pond, then warmth and light made algae multiply," said Priya. "Hence the green water."

In their report, the students described the outcome and suggested a fix: a strip of tall grass between the field and the pond to catch the runoff. The water was still cloudy in June due to nutrients left in the mud, but the principal agreed to plant the strip. The class would measure the results next spring.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the phrase "where the problem might originate" most nearly means where the problem
choices: could be fixed
might be forgotten
might begin
was most dangerous
qs.why: The class is looking for the starting point of the problem, and then finds the drainage pipe and the fertilizer.

qs.q: What role did the week of warm, sunny weather play?
choices: It set off a burst of algae growth after the fertilizer had reached the pond.
It carried the fertilizer from the field to the pond.
It removed oxygen from the pond water.
It caused the groundskeeper to fertilize the field.
qs.why: The weather triggered the algae growth, but the fertilizer was already in the pond because of the rain and the pipe.

qs.q: Which detail best explains how the fertilizer reached the pond?
choices: The pond was behind the school.
The groundskeeper fertilized the field in the spring.
Algae use sunlight to grow.
Heavy rain washed some of the fertilizer through a drainage pipe that emptied into the pond.
qs.why: The pipe from the field and the heavy rain together show the path the fertilizer took.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, Priya's words "Hence the green water" most nearly mean
choices: the water will soon be clear
which is why the water turned green
the water was green before the rain
no one knows why the water is green
qs.why: Priya has just explained the chain of causes, so hence introduces the result: the green water.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Fertilizer should never be used near schools.
Algae are always harmful to fish.
A chain of causes made the pond turn green, and the class suggested a way to reduce the problem.
Ms. Chavez was the first to notice the green pond.
qs.why: The passage explains the steps from fertilizer to green water and ends with a proposed fix.

write.prompt: Describe a chain of causes and effects you have seen at home, at school, or in nature. Use at least three words from this unit, including one connector (thus, hence, or due to).
write.frame: It started when ___ triggered ___. ___ contributed to the result, and thus ___.

study.task: Draw a chain of four boxes showing causes and effects from the passage or from your life. Label the first box with originate, label one arrow with trigger, and write one sentence under the chain that uses thus, hence, or due to.

sentences: Write a sentence that uses outcome to describe the result of a game, a vote, or an experiment.
Write a sentence that names something that could trigger an event, and name the event.
Write a sentence that uses due to followed by a noun that names a cause.

given: A spark landed in dry grass.
combine.model: A single spark in dry grass triggered a fire that spread quickly.

discuss: Can something be a trigger without being the real cause? Use trigger and contribute in your answer.
How can the same event have a good impact on one person and a bad impact on another?
Why do writers use thus and hence instead of so? When would so be better?
produce.explain: Explain a chain of causes and effects from the passage or from your life. Use at least two of these words: thus, hence, due to.

argue.prompt: Claim: Friends have more influence than ads on what students choose to wear. Take a side and support it with two reasons using words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. The strongest influence on ___ is ___, due to ___.

constructed.prompt: Describe how a small event could start a larger problem at a school, such as a crowded hallway. Use trigger, contribute, and outcome.
look: shows at least one other factor and a result
constructed.model: A dropped box of pencils could trigger a pile-up in a crowded hallway. The narrow space and the late bell contributed to the problem. The outcome was that several students were late to class.

constructed.prompt: Write three connected sentences about a canceled field trip. Use thus, hence, and due to correctly.
look: uses due to before a noun phrase
shows a clear cause-and-effect link in each sentence
constructed.model: The trip was canceled due to a bus shortage. The school could not rent another bus; thus, the class stayed at school. The students planned a school-yard picnic instead, hence the lunches in the courtyard.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words and phrases for causes, triggers, and results, read a science passage about a pond that turned green, practice telling apart a trigger, a contributing factor, and an outcome, and use thus, hence, and due to correctly in formal writing.

notes.va.outcome.n: Outcome is a compound of out and come: what comes out of something. Students sometimes use it for what a person hopes for; the word names what actually happened. Ask for an expected outcome and an actual outcome.
notes.va.trigger.v: A trigger starts a chain, but it is not always the whole cause. Use a row of dominoes: the first tap is the trigger and the standing row is the deeper cause. Keep examples neutral; the word is also used for emotional triggers, which this unit does not teach.
notes.va.contribute.v: Contribute covers two uses: giving to a shared effort and adding to a result. Both mean a part of a whole. Contrast with trigger: a trigger starts something, while contributing factors add to it.
notes.va.influence.n: Influence is a quiet cause: it shapes choices without forcing them. Show the noun and the verb together. Distinguish it from control, which includes force.
notes.va.impact.n: Impact moves from the physical sense (one thing hitting another) to any strong effect. It can be good or bad; ask for adjectives that go with it, such as positive, harmful, lasting. Do not accept impact for any small change.
notes.va.provoke.v: Provoke is a trigger with emotion attached: it names the reaction. Notice the second root meaning 'call': to call forth a reaction. Ask whether provoking is always negative; it can be neutral, as in provoking thought.
notes.va.originate.v: Originate names the starting point of a chain; trigger names what sets it off. A rumor can originate in one place and be triggered by another event. Use the family word origin to anchor the meaning.
notes.va.thus.adv: Thus is a formal result word, close to therefore. It often follows a semicolon or a comma. It can also mean 'in this way', which this unit does not teach. Students overuse it; ask for a sentence where the cause really leads to the result.
notes.va.hence.adv: Hence is often followed by a noun phrase (hence the name) rather than a full clause. It is formal and appears in science and history texts. Hence can also mean 'from now' in older writing; ignore that sense for this unit.
notes.va.due-to.phr: Due to is followed by a noun phrase (due to the storm); because is followed by a clause (because it stormed). This is the most common error in formal writing. Have students rewrite sentences with because of, due to, and because.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The passage says a week of warm weather triggered a burst of algae growth. A trigger sets something off, but the fertilizer was already there, so the weather is not the only cause. Then it says these causes contributed to the bloom. Contribute tells me each cause added a part.'
discuss: In a chain of events, how do you decide which event is the trigger and which is the deeper cause?
Why might a writer choose due to instead of because? What changes in the sentence?
misconceptions: A trigger is always the main cause of an event.
Due to and because can be swapped in any sentence.
Thus and hence can connect any two sentences, even unrelated ones.
extend: Choose a historical event and write a three-box chain that shows its origin, a trigger, and an outcome.
Find three sentences in a science article that use cause words and rewrite them with different words from the unit.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit gradual and emerge from unit 5 and logical from grade 5: ask how a gradual change can contribute to a later trigger, how a pattern emerges from several causes, and whether a cause-and-effect claim is logical. Check recall at two days and one week.

wida.oral: Partner A names a cause and Partner B says the effect using thus. Then they switch and use due to with a noun.

needsReview: Science claims in the passage believed accurate: nutrient runoff from fertilizer can feed algae growth; warm, sunny weather speeds algae growth; when algae die, organisms that break them down can use up oxygen; a strip of tall grass can catch runoff. A science reviewer should confirm the wording.
Morphology: provoke is shown as pro- (forth) plus vok (call) with a silent e; origin plus -ate for originate. Confirm the wording of the root and prefix meanings.
Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: desencadenar (trigger), por lo tanto (thus), de ahí (hence), debido a (due to), originarse.
Usage note: due to before a noun phrase and because before a clause reflects a traditional rule that not all style guides enforce; confirm the teacher note is not too prescriptive.
Sense boundary: trigger (noun), influence (verb), impact (physical force) are second senses; confirm they help rather than distract.
